title: Water
strapline: Pouring, floating, freezing, flowing — the everyday material that never behaves the same way twice.
intent: Master pouring — the tilt, the aim, the stop — from splashy two-handed jug work to filling a doll's cup to the brim without a drop lost.
Investigate floating and sinking, and start predicting: heavy things don't always sink, and children need to meet that surprise for themselves.
Watch materials change state — ice melting in warm hands, puddles disappearing in the sun, bubbles appearing when air is whisked in.
Explore how water moves through things — tubes, pumps, water wheels, guttering, holes in the bottom of a cup.
Feel capacity in the hands and arms: full is heavy, empty is light, and 'nearly full' is a judgement call.
Find calm — water play regulates as well as it teaches, and some children come to the tray to settle.
implementation: Give the pour time and dignity: real jugs, real cups, a tea-towel for spills, and no rush — pouring your own drink at snack is where this learning lands.
Set up float-and-sink as a genuine investigation, not a quiz: gather objects with the children, take predictions first, and be delighted when the heavy log floats.
Freeze things — coloured water, small-world figures, flowers — and hand the ice over without instructions; rescue missions invent themselves.
Narrate what water does in plain words: drip, trickle, gush, overflow, soak, absorb, melt.
Follow the water outdoors: puddles after rain, painting the fence with big brushes and watching the marks vanish, watering the plants that actually need it.
Let babies lead with their whole bodies — splashing, patting, mouthing cups — with an adult close and towels closer.
Change the water's character across the week: warm and soapy for washing dolls, icy with bergs, tinted, herbal — same tray, new thinking.
key_questions: Do you think it will float or sink — why?
How can we get the water from here to there without carrying it?
What's happening to the ice — can you make it melt faster?
Which holds more, the tall thin one or the short fat one?
How does the warm water feel different from the cold?

impact.text: Babies pat, splash and swirl water for the pure joy of the sensation, watching drips from their own fingers.
Toddlers fill and empty containers over and over, delighting in 'all gone' and asking for more.
Children pour between containers with growing control, and older children fill a cup right to the line without spilling.
Children work out the water toys as machines — pressing the pump, angling the guttering, feeding the wheel — and fix the run when it stalls.
Children explore floating, sinking and melting first-hand, adding ice to warm water to watch it disappear faster.
Children make predictions before dropping objects in, and ask real questions when the result surprises them.
Children compare containers and amounts as they pour — this one holds more, that one's nearly full, mine's heavier.
Children fold water into pretend play — washing the baby, making cups of tea, cooking soup for a friend.

enhancements: A frozen 'berg' with small-world penguins locked inside, plus salt, warm water and droppers for the rescue.
Clear tubing, funnels and a hand pump clamped to the tray — engineering the water uphill.
Washing day: warm soapy water, dolls, cloths and a real washing line with pegs.
A basket of float-or-sink objects chosen to mislead — a big cork, a small coin, an orange with and without its peel.
Big decorating brushes and buckets of plain water for fence and playground 'painting' on dry days.
Measuring jugs, ladles and a marked 'fill to here' line to bring number and precision to the pouring.
Guttering and drainpipes on the fence at different slopes — race the water, then re-rig the course.

playing_exploring: Water invites having-a-go at every age — there is no wrong way in, and every action gets an instant, visible response.
Children carry familiar routines into the tray — washing, cooking, watering — and stretch them into new stories.
active_learning: Getting the water wheel to spin, or the cup filled without spilling, takes repeated, self-corrected effort.
Children stay remarkably long at water — the material holds attention and rewards another try.
creating_thinking: Predict, test, revise: float-and-sink and melting ice are children's first real experiments.
They link ideas across contexts — the puddle, the kettle steam, the melting berg — and start building theories about how water behaves.
